reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, often after a preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
Regarded as a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome and part of the anti-GQ1b antibody spectrum
Serum anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in the great majority of cases and strongly support the diagnosis
Consciousness is preserved, distinguishing it from Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis, which shares the anti-GQ1b mechanism but adds encephalopathy
Cerebrospinal fluid often shows albuminocytological dissociation, though this may be absent early
Overlap with limb-weakness Guillain-Barre syndrome can occur, so monitoring for respiratory and bulbar involvement is important
Treatment mirrors Guillain-Barre syndrome using intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with many patients also recovering spontaneously
reference.pathophysiology: Miller Fisher syndrome is an acute immune-mediated neuropathy triggered by infection, in which antibodies against the GQ1b ganglioside are generated through molecular mimicry with microbial (often Campylobacter jejuni) lipo-oligosaccharide. GQ1b is densely expressed in the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves and in muscle-spindle afferents, so antibody binding there produces ophthalmoplegia and sensory ataxia, while impaired large-fibre afferent function causes areflexia. The peripheral, largely nodal-paranodal site of injury and the self-limiting immune response underlie the generally favourable outcome.
additionalInvestigations: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for albuminocytological dissociation
Nerve conduction studies, which may show reduced sensory responses or subtle changes
MRI of the brain to exclude brainstem lesions when the picture is atypical
Screening for preceding Campylobacter or other infection
Respiratory function monitoring where overlap weakness is suspected
redFlags: Evolving limb weakness or respiratory compromise indicating overlap with Guillain-Barre syndrome
Bulbar dysfunction threatening swallowing and the airway
Declining consciousness suggesting Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis
Rapid deterioration requiring escalation of care
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering fully over weeks to months, though those with overlapping Guillain-Barre features may have a more prolonged course.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign course and missing evolving respiratory or bulbar weakness
Attributing ophthalmoplegia to myasthenia or stroke
Excluding the diagnosis when early cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal
Overlooking the encephalopathy that would reclassify the case as Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat with immunotherapy, either intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, particularly where there is significant disability or Guillain-Barre overlap
Monitor respiratory and bulbar function closely for overlapping Guillain-Barre weakness, escalating to ventilatory support if required
Provide supportive care including venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and physiotherapy during recovery
Manage the ophthalmoplegia symptomatically with monocular occlusion for diplopia and ocular lubrication
Watch for and treat autonomic instability
Manage under neurology and neuroimmunology, reassuring that recovery is usually complete over weeks to months
